title: ESXi Administration Command
summary: This technique abuses the guest management services that virtualisation platforms install inside virtual machines so the host can look after them. A background agent runs in each guest and exposes remote operations, which on Windows guests appears as a tools daemon process, with equivalent daemons on Linux and macOS. An actor who has reached the ESXi host or its management plane can use those channels to act inside every guest that trusts the host, without any guest credentials. Programmatic access runs through the platform's web services interfaces, where calls such as starting a program in a guest, listing processes, listing files, or initiating a file transfer from a guest provide execution, discovery and collection in one place. The critical detection point is direction: the guest's own logs show actions with no interactive login, no network session from the usual workstation, and a parent process that is the tools daemon. Command execution recorded by the guest operating system will name the tools daemon as the originating process rather than a shell or a user session, and management plane logs on the host will show the corresponding task. Because administrators legitimately use these interfaces for automation, the differentiators are the calling account, the source of the request, the volume of operations, and whether the guest-side activity matches any sanctioned change.

beginner.definition: This is when an attacker uses the software a virtualisation host puts inside each virtual machine to run commands. That software exists so the host can manage its guests, for example to shut them down cleanly. An attacker who controls the host can therefore run commands in every guest. They do not need any password for the guest itself.
beginner.whyItMatters: One compromised virtualisation host can mean access to every machine running on it. For an attacker, that is a very large step up. The commands run through management software are designed to be quiet, so they leave no login record in the guest. That makes them easy to miss if you only watch for normal remote logins. From there, an attacker can collect files, dump credentials and prepare for wider damage.
howItWorks: The attacker gains control of an ESXi host or of the management interface that controls it.
They locate the management service that runs inside each guest, which is installed with the virtualisation tools.
They call a platform interface that starts a program inside the guest, naming the guest and the command.
They may instead list running processes or files, or request a file transfer that copies data out of the guest.
The guest performs these actions without a user logging in, so no password is checked.
The attacker repeats this across other guests on the same host, widening their reach.
beginner.example: Picture an apartment building where the caretaker holds a master service key for every flat. The key is there so he can fix leaks when nobody is at home. If a criminal copies that key, he can enter every flat, open drawers and carry things out. No tenant ever unlocks a door for him, so their own doorbell logs stay empty. From the outside, it looks exactly like routine maintenance.
takeaways: Guest management agents let a host act inside every virtual machine it runs.
Actions through those agents need no guest login, so watch host side logs too.
Look for commands whose parent process is the virtualisation tools daemon.

objectives: Explain what a guest management agent is and why it exists on virtual machines.
Describe how a compromised host can execute commands inside guests without guest credentials.
List the kinds of operations available, such as run program, list files and transfer files.
Identify the guest side and host side logs that record these operations.
Explain why legitimate administration makes context, not the command, the deciding factor.
